label: thm:fixed-host
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fixed-host}
With the notation above, for every fixed $r\ge3$ there are constants
$A_r,B_r,R_r<\infty$ with the following property.
Let $\Gamma=\Gamma_n$ be a sequence of simple $r$-uniform
hypergraphs and let $D=D_n\to\infty$.  Put
\[
 \delta_n:=\max_{v\in V(\Gamma)}
       \left|\frac{d_v}{D}-1\right|,
 \qquad
 T_D:=\frac{\log(1+(r-1)D)}{r-1}.
\]
Suppose that for fixed $q>2$ and $C,L,K<\infty$ the following
conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \emph{Size and stability:}
\[
 N\le D^K,
 \qquad
 \|e^{-(r-1)t\mathsf T}\|_{L^q(\pi)\to L^q(\pi)}
 \le C(1+t)^L\quad(0\le t\le T_D).
\]
\item \emph{Near-regularity and small stability error:}
$\delta_n\to0$ and
\[
 N^{1/q}\left(\delta_n+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
 (1+\log D)^{2L+2}=o(1).
\]
\item \emph{Small collision errors:}
\[
 D^{A_r}\chi_{R_r}(\Gamma)+\frac{D^{B_r}}{M}
 =o\!\left(D^{-2/(r-1)}\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then, writing $Q_D(1)=(1+(r-1)D)^{-1/(r-1)}$, we have
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{Z_\Gamma}{NQ_D(1)}-1\right)^2\right]=o(1).
\]
In particular, $Z_\Gamma/(NQ_D(1))\to1$ in probability.

label: lem:finite-query
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-query}
Every call $\mathsf{Test}(S,t;P)$, with $P=\bot$ or $U_P=t$,
returns true exactly when all resources in $S$ are free before $t$.
In particular, $X_v=\mathsf{Test}(\{v\},1;\bot)$.
head: environment
name: Correctness of the finite query

title: Proof
body_md:
Induct on the number of  candidate priorities below $t$;
every recursive call has a smaller threshold.  If all resources in
$S$ are free before $t$, a true recursive call at an entry $(u,A)$
with $U_A<t$ would say, by induction, that the other resources of $A$
are free before $U_A$.  Since $u$ is free as well, $A$ would have been
accepted, a contradiction.  Thus the test returns true.

Conversely, if a resource of $S$ is covered before $t$, choose an
accepted candidate $A$ meeting $S$ with $U_A<t$ and $u\in A\cap S$.
The entry $(u,A)$ is in the scanner: an omitted incoming candidate
has priority $t$, not less than $t$.  All resources of
$A\setminus\{u\}$ were free before $U_A$, so induction says that
this entry's recursive call returns true.  The test therefore returns
false.  The argument also covers repeated entries of one candidate
in a merged scanner.

label: lem:finite-determination
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-determination}
For every typed incidence cover, every priority horizon $x\in[0,1]$, and every
fixed finite set of nodes, all decisions concerning those nodes before time
$x$ are determined by a finite random neighbourhood almost surely.
head: environment
name: Finite determination

title: Proof
body_md:
Each candidate occurrence has at most $B$ candidate grandchildren,
for some finite bound $B$.  A prescribed chain of $\ell+1$ candidate
occurrences can be a dependency chain only if their independent
priorities decrease, with probability $1/(\ell+1)!$.  There are at
most $B^\ell$ such chains starting at any fixed occurrence, and
$B^\ell/(\ell+1)!\to0$.  Thus every fixed finite collection of decisions has a finite
dependency neighbourhood almost surely.

label: lem:candidate-first
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Candidate repetitions precede resource repetitions

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose a second occurrence of resource type $u$ is born from an
invoked candidate occurrence of type $A$.  The complete scanner of
the earlier $u$ has already been exposed: every batch of forward
resources has its scanners exposed before any further candidate is
invoked, and distinct forward resources of one candidate have
distinct types.  Let $P$ be the earlier occurrence's incoming
candidate type, or $\bot$ if it is the root.  If $A\ne P$, the
earlier scanner exposed an occurrence of type $A$; if $A=P$, the
incoming candidate of the earlier occurrence was already exposed.
In the first case this earlier occurrence is distinct from the
one now invoked: a candidate entered through type $u$ cannot
produce another forward resource of type $u$.  In the second case
the incoming candidate is likewise a distinct occurrence.  Thus
type $A$ repeats before the second birth of $u$.

label: lem:direct-coupling
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:direct-coupling}
For each fixed resource $v$, the finite-query answer $X_v$ and the
independent-cover answer $Y_v$ can be coupled so that
\[
 \mathbb P(X_v\ne Y_v)\le\mathbb P(\mathcal C_v).
\]
head: environment
name: First-label coupling

title: Proof
body_md:
Sample the actual priorities $(U_A:A\in E(\Gamma))$ independently
and uniformly.  Explore $\mathcal T_v$ in the prescribed scanner
order.  When an occurrence of  candidate type $A$ is exposed
for the first time, give it priority $U_A$; for every later exposed
occurrence of type $A$, use a fresh independent uniform priority.
Complete the unused occurrence priorities independently.

This produces the correct independent-cover law.  Immediately
before each exposure, the type to be exposed is determined by the
previously revealed information and the fixed scanner order.  If its
type is new, $U_A$ is still unread and independent of that history;
otherwise the assigned priority is fresh.  Induction over exposures
therefore gives independent uniform priorities to all cover
occurrences, without conditioning on $\mathcal C_v^c$.

On $\mathcal C_v^c$, every exposed cover priority equals the actual
priority of its type.  Lemma~\ref{lem:candidate-first} also makes
all registered resource types distinct.  Consequently the actual
and cover queries encounter the same complete scanners and use the
same priorities.  Their recursive answers agree by induction over
the almost surely finite dependency neighbourhood of
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-determination}.  Hence $X_v=Y_v$ on
$\mathcal C_v^c$, proving the bound.

label: eq:cavity-integral
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f_{A\to v}^{[h]}$ denote the branch message with $h$ remaining
candidate generations and free boundary resources.  Write
$q_{u\to A}^{[h-1]}$ for its child cavity messages.  The branch
through $A$ consumes $v$ at priority $t$ if and only if the other
resource children are free immediately before $t$.  Their subtrees are
disjoint, so for $h\ge1$,
\[
 f_{A\to v}^{[h]}(x)
 =1-\int_0^x
 \prod_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}q_{u\to A}^{[h-1]}(t)\,dt.
\]
The child messages have index $h-1$, not $h$.  Almost-sure finite
determination gives pointwise convergence of these probabilities; bounded
convergence therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cavity-integral}
 f_{A\to v}(x)
 =1-\int_0^x
 \prod_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}q_{u\to A}(t)\,dt.
\end{equation}
The branch messages are continuous by \eqref{eq:cavity-integral}, as are their finite products
$q_{u\to A}$.  We may therefore differentiate \eqref{eq:cavity-integral}, obtaining \eqref{eq:cavity-branch-derivative}.
Differentiating \eqref{eq:cavity-root-survival} for the limiting messages gives
\[
 q'_v
 =
 \sum_{A\ni v}f'_{A\to v}
 \prod_{C\ni v,\,C\ne A}f_{C\to v}
 =-
 \sum_{A\ni v}
 q_{v\to A}
 \prod_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}q_{u\to A},
\]
which is \eqref{eq:cavity-root-derivative}.

label: eq:duhamel-prefix
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $y(0)=0$, Duhamel's formula and
Lemma~\ref{lem:linearized} give, on every $[0,t]$ on which
$\|y\|_\infty\le h_0$,
\[
 y(\tau)=\int_0^\tau e^{-(r-1)(\tau-s)\mathsf T}
 \left(y'(s)+(r-1)\mathsf Ty(s)\right)\,ds.
\]
Near regularity gives $\pi_{\min}\ge c/N$, so
$\|z\|_\infty\le C_3N^{1/q}\|z\|_{L^q(\pi)}$.
Write $Y(\tau)=\sup_{0\le s\le\tau}\|y(s)\|_{L^q(\pi)}$.
The hypothesis and \eqref{eq:residual-bound} yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:duhamel-prefix}
 Y(\tau)\le C_2(1+T_D)^{L+1}
 \left[\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}
       +C_3N^{1/q}Y(\tau)^2\right].
\end{equation}

Fix $C_1>2C_2$.  We claim that
\[
 Y(\tau)\le 2C_1(1+T_D)^{L+1}
             \left(\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
 \qquad (0\le\tau<T_D).
\]
Initially $y(0)=0$.  On any $[0,t]$ satisfying this bound and
$\|y\|_\infty\le h_0$, substitution into
\eqref{eq:duhamel-prefix} gives
\[
 Y(\tau)\le C_2(1+T_D)^{L+1}
 \left(\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
 \left[1+4C_3C_1^2N^{1/q}
       \left(\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
       (1+T_D)^{2L+2}\right].
\]
The bracket is $1+o(1)$ by \eqref{eq:bootstrap-assumption}.
Thus the preceding bound improves to at most
$\frac32C_1(1+T_D)^{L+1}(\delta+\log D/D)$. 
On the same $[0,t]$ we deduce
\[
 \|y\|_\infty\le 2C_1C_3N^{1/q}(1+T_D)^{L+1}
                    \left(\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
 =o(1)<h_0/2.
\]
The residual estimate has only been used under its hypothesis on $[0,t]$,
If either bootstrap bound failed before $T_D$,
continuity of the finite message products and their positivity for
$x<1$ would permit both strict improvements to persist past the
first failure.  Hence the bounds hold for all $\tau<T_D$.
In particular,
\[
 \sup_{\substack{0\le x<1\\v\in V(\Gamma)}}
 \left|\log\frac{q_v(x)}{Q_D(x)}\right|
 \le C_{r,C,L,q}N^{1/q}
 \left(\delta+\frac{\log D}{D}\right)
 (1+\log D)^{L+1}=o(1).
\]
The message estimate gives $f_{A\to v}(x)\ge3/4$ for $x<1$,
and hence also at $x=1$ by continuity.  Thus
$q_v(1)=\prod_{A\ni v}f_{A\to v}(1)>0$, so the logarithms and
bounds extend to $x=1$.  Now $q_v=Q_D e^{y_v}$ proves
\eqref{eq:cover-survival-asymptotic}, and the message estimate gives
\eqref{eq:message-near-one}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Until a message first reaches $3/4$, equations \eqref{eq:cavity-branch-derivative}, \eqref{eq:cavity-omitted-survival}, and
\eqref{eq:deviation-definition} give
\[
 |f'_{A\to v}(x)|
 \le
 \left(\frac43e^{h_0}Q_D(x)\right)^{r-1}
 \le C_rQ_D(x)^{r-1}.
\]
Since $Q_D(t)^{r-1}=1/(1+(r-1)Dt)$, integration gives
\[
 1-f_{A\to v}(x)
 \le C_r\int_0^xQ_D(t)^{r-1}\,dt
 \le C_r\frac{\log(1+(r-1)D)}{(r-1)D}
 =O_r\!\left(\frac{\log D}{D}\right).
\]

from reaching $3/4$ and proving \eqref{eq:message-correction}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $A\ni v$, write
\[
 z_{A,v}:=\sum_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}y_u,
 \qquad
 m_A:=\prod_{u\in A}f_{A\to u}^{-1}.
\]
By the message estimate, $m_A=1+O_r(\log D/D)$ uniformly.  For $\|y\|_\infty\le h_0$, Taylor's theorem gives
\[
 |e^{z_{A,v}}-1-z_{A,v}|
 \le
 C_r\|y\|_\infty
 \sum_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}|y_u|.
\]
The cross term $(m_A-1)z_{A,v}$ has absolute value at most
$C_r(\log D/D)\sum_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}|y_u|$.
Since $\|y\|_\infty\le h_0<1$ and $d_v=O_r(D)$, summing over
$A\ni v$ and dividing by $D$ contributes $O_r(\log D/D)$, which
is included in the additive error rather than the quadratic remainder.

Substituting in \eqref{eq:log-derivative},
\[
 \frac{dy_v}{d\tau}
 =1-\frac{d_v}{D}
 -\frac1D\sum_{A\ni v}
 \sum_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}y_u
 +E_v,
\]
where
\[
 |E_v|
 \le
 C_r\left[
 \frac{d_v}{D}\frac{\log D}{D}
 +\frac{\|y\|_\infty}{D}
 \sum_{A\ni v}\sum_{u\in A\setminus\{v\}}|y_u|
 \right].
\]
The middle linear term is $-(r-1)(d_v/D)(\mathsf T y)(v)$.
Consequently, the residual in \eqref{eq:residual-bound} satisfies
\[
 (y'+(r-1)\mathsf Ty)_v
 =\left(1-\frac{d_v}{D}\right)
  \left(1+(r-1)(\mathsf T y)(v)\right)+E_v.
\]
Since $\|y\|_{L^q(\pi)}\le\|y\|_\infty\le1$ and the stationary
Markov operator $\mathsf T$ is a contraction on $L^q(\pi)$, taking
norms of this identity and the bound on $E_v$ proves \eqref{eq:residual-bound}.

label: thm:transfer
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Collision comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:cavity-stability} gives
\[
 q_v(1)=(1+o(1))Q_D(1)
 =(1+o(1))((r-1)D)^{-1/(r-1)}.
\]
Thus $\bar q=(1+o(1))Q_D(1)$, and the two bounds \eqref{eq:cover-survival-bounds} hold for
sufficiently large $n$.

Let $\alpha_r,\gamma_r$ be supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}.
Choose $\kappa_r>\alpha_r+2/(r-1)+2$ and set
$R_r:=4\kappa_r+8$.  Enlarge the exponents in the statement of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-host}, if necessary, to satisfy
\[
 A_r>\alpha_r+1,\qquad B_r>\gamma_r+1.
\]
Since $B=\Theta_r(D)$, the anchored-counting contribution obeys
$R_0^{\alpha_r}B^{-\kappa_r}=o(D^{-2/(r-1)})$.
The short-cycle hypothesis gives
$\chi_{R_r}R_0^{\alpha_r}=o(D^{-2/(r-1)})$,
while $D^{B_r}/M=o(D^{-2/(r-1)})$ controls the cross-root term.
Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer} gives
$|\mathbb E(Z/N)-\bar q|=o(D^{-2/(r-1)})$ and
$|\mathbb E[(Z/N)^2]-\bar q^2|=o(D^{-2/(r-1)})$.
As $\bar q=(1+o(1))Q_D(1)$ and
$Q_D(1)^2=\Theta_r(D^{-2/(r-1)})$, the moment bound
\eqref{eq:moment-L2-bridge} gives
$\mathbb E[(Z/(NQ_D(1))-1)^2]=o(1)$.
The expectation, variance and convergence-in-probability assertions
follow.

body_md:
\label{lem:private-block}
Let $\kappa\ge2$, $R=4\kappa+8$, and fix a two-path shape with
$L$ successive-invocation steps and distance greater than $R$
between $x$ and $y$ in the incidence tree.  There are at most $C_rNR_0^4(K_rB)^LB^{-\kappa}$ first-collision

head: environment
name: Anchored count for long first collisions

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:moment-first} and \eqref{eq:moment-second}, it suffices to prove \eqref{eq:first-collision-bound} and \eqref{eq:cross-root-collision}.
Take the first repeated candidate type and its earlier occurrence.
The paths to the two selected occurrences form a first-collision witness.
If their connecting path has at most $R$ incidence edges, its 
image closes to a simple incidence cycle of length at most $R$:
all interior candidate and resource types are distinct, while
the two selected candidates have the same type.  Let $\mathcal C_R$ be
the set of candidate types on such cycles, and let $\mathcal B_R$
be the event that a uniform-root cover query exposes a type in
$\mathcal C_R$.  Since $|\mathcal C_R|=M\chi_R$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:one-label-exposure} gives
\[
 \mathbb P(\mathcal B_R)
 \le\sum_{A\in\mathcal C_R}p_A
 \le\frac{C_r|\mathcal C_R|R_0^{H_r}}N
 \le C_r\chi_RR_0^{H_r+1}.
\]

Let $\mathcal W_R$ be the set of long first-collision witnesses,
rooted at arbitrary resource types, whose selected paths contain no
type in $\mathcal C_R$.  For each such witness $W$ rooted at $v$,
write $\mathcal V_W$ for the event that the cover query rooted at $v$
exposes its two selected candidate occurrences.  If a first repetition
is not accounted for by $\mathcal B_R$, it gives a witness in
$\mathcal W_R$.  Thus
$p_{\mathrm{rep}}\le\mathbb P(\mathcal B_R)+N^{-1}
\sum_{W\in\mathcal W_R}\mathbb P(\mathcal V_W)$.
For each unlabelled shape, multiply the count in
Lemma~\ref{lem:private-block} by the visitation bound in
Lemma~\ref{lem:two-path-visit}, average over roots, and sum shapes
and lengths.  There are at most $K_r^{L+1}$ shapes for
$h,\ell_1,\ell_2$, so
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_{W\in\mathcal W_R}\mathbb P(\mathcal V_W)
 &\le C_rR_0^7B^{-\kappa}\sum_{h,\ell_1,\ell_2\ge0}
   \frac{(K_r^2B\mu_D)^{h+\ell_1+\ell_2}}{h!\ell_1!\ell_2!}\\
 &=C_rR_0^7B^{-\kappa}\exp(3K_r^2B\mu_D).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Since $B\mu_D\le\frac32c_r\log R_0$, this is at most
$C_rR_0^{7+(9/2)c_rK_r^2}B^{-\kappa}$.
Choose any integer
$\alpha_r>\max\{H_r+1,\,7+(9/2)c_rK_r^2\}$.
Combining the two cases establishes \eqref{eq:first-collision-bound}.

Independence of the two roots and their occurrence priorities gives
\[
 p_{\mathrm{shared}}\le\sum_{A\in E(\Gamma)}p_A^2
 \le\frac{C_rMR_0^{2H_r}}{N^2}.
\]
Since $rM=\sum_vd_v$ and $d_v\le3D/2$,
$M/N\le C_rD$, whence
$M/N^2\le C_rR_0^2/M$.
Taking any integer $\gamma_r>2H_r+2$ establishes \eqref{eq:cross-root-collision}.

Substituting \eqref{eq:first-collision-bound} and \eqref{eq:cross-root-collision} into \eqref{eq:moment-first} and \eqref{eq:moment-second} proves
\eqref{eq:collision-moment-first}--\eqref{eq:collision-moment-second}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $W$ before sampling priorities.  Let $I(W)$ be the required
invoked candidate occurrences, and let $\mathcal V_W$ be the event
that the query exposes $x,y$.  Write $E(W)$ for the steps $A\to C$
between successive required invocations; thus
$|E(W)|=h+\ell_1+\ell_2$.  At most one candidate invocation below
the root has two required successors.  Let $E_{\rm br}$ consist of
its outgoing steps, if any, so $|E_{\rm br}|\le2$.

Fix the vector $U_I=(U_C)_{C\in I(W)}$ at
$t=(t_C)_{C\in I(W)}\in[0,1]^{I(W)}$.  Write $\mathbb P_{\rm off}$
for probability over the remaining independent occurrence priorities,
and $\mathcal V_W(t)$ for the exposure event with $U_I=t$.
Put $\mathcal D_W=\{t:t_C<t_A\text{ for all }(A,C)\in E(W)\}$.
The event $\mathcal V_W(t)$ is impossible unless $t\in\mathcal D_W$.

Set $w(s)=c_rQ_D(s)^{r-1}=c_r/(1+(r-1)Ds)$, so that
$\mu_D=\int_0^1w(s)\,ds$.  Consider a step $A\to C$ with
$C$ the only required successor of $A$.  Let $p$ be the incoming
resource of $A$, and $u$ the forward resource whose scanner contains
$C$.  For $C$ to be invoked at priority $t_C$, all other entries of
priority below $t_C$ in the merged forward scanner of $A$ must
return false.  Given $U_I=t$, these answers depend only on the
candidate branches other than $A$ and $C$ at $u$, and other than $A$
at each $z\in A\setminus\{p,u\}$.  By the cavity product
\eqref{eq:cavity-root-survival}, their joint probability is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\frac{q_u(t_C)}{f_{A\to u}(t_C)f_{C\to u}(t_C)}
   \prod_{z\in A\setminus\{p,u\}}
      \frac{q_z(t_C)}{f_{A\to z}(t_C)}\\
 &\qquad\le \frac{20}{9}Q_D(t_C)
       \left(\frac53Q_D(t_C)\right)^{r-2}
       =w(t_C).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, those branches are distinct in the incidence cover, even
if some have the same  candidate type.  For different ordinary
steps, they lie in disjoint subtrees off the selected paths, so their
scanner outcomes are conditionally independent.

We discard all root-scanner conditions and the conditions at the
possible branching invocation.  By the preceding calculation,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P_{\rm off}(\mathcal V_W(t))
 &\le\mathbf1_{\mathcal D_W}(t)
      \prod_{(A,C)\in E(W)\setminus E_{\rm br}}w(t_C)\\
 &\le \left(\frac{R_0}{c_r}\right)^2
      \mathbf1_{\mathcal D_W}(t)
      \prod_{(A,C)\in E(W)}w(t_C),
 \end{aligned}
\]
since $w(s)\ge c_r/R_0$ and $|E_{\rm br}|\le2$.

Integrate over the independent priorities in $I(W)$.  Dropping
ordering constraints between the common chain and its two
continuations allows three decreasing-priority integrals; the
at most two root-invoked candidates contribute unweighted integrals
of at most one.  Hence
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P(\mathcal V_W)
 &=\int_{[0,1]^{I(W)}}\mathbb P_{\rm off}(\mathcal V_W(t))
                     \prod_{C\in I(W)}dt_C\\
 &\le \left(\frac{R_0}{c_r}\right)^2
      \int_{\mathcal D_W}\prod_{(A,C)\in E(W)}w(t_C)
                            \prod_{C\in I(W)}dt_C\\
 &\le \left(\frac{R_0}{c_r}\right)^2
      \frac{\mu_D^{h+\ell_1+\ell_2}}{h!\,\ell_1!\,\ell_2!}
 \le C_rR_0^3\frac{\mu_D^{h+\ell_1+\ell_2}}{h!\,\ell_1!\,\ell_2!}.
 \end{aligned}\qedhere
\]

The root scanner exposes $A$ only if the uniform root is one of its

exposed in the scanner of a resource $u$ born from an invoked candidate

a block
\[

strictly after $z$, with $x$ exposed through $Y-u-x$.

Retain the root, the incidence choices outside the open interior of
this block, and the candidate type $A$ of the other selected occurrence
$y$.  Since $x$ has the same type $A$, specifying its terminal scanner
requires choosing $u\in A$ and $Y\ni u$, in at most $rd_*$ ways.

$A_0,Y$.  There are $N$ choices for the root, at most two initial
candidates and two terminal scanner entries giving at most four
degree-sized choices, and at most $K_rB$ incidence choices for each

most $C_rNR_0^4(K_rB)^{L-\kappa}$ encodings.

candidates would be connected by two distinct simple  incidence

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $F$ be a fixed strictly $k$-balanced $k$-uniform hypergraph, with
$m=v(F)$, $r=e(F)$, and $\rho_F=(r-1)/(m-k)$.  Define
\[
 C_F=\frac1{k!}
 \left(\frac{r(r-1)k!}{\operatorname{aut}(F)}\right)^{-1/(r-1)}.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{e(H_{\mathrm{fin}})}{n^{k-1/\rho_F}}-C_F\right)^2\right]
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular, $e(H_{\mathrm{fin}})=(C_F+o_{\mathbb P}(1))n^{k-1/\rho_F}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-host} conditionally on the handoff.
Its hypotheses are near-regular resource degrees, stability of the
resource walk and short-cycle sparsity, with the stated quantitative
smallness conditions.  The degree estimate is
Corollary~\ref{cor:near-regular-handoff}; the other two are
Theorems~\ref{thm:resource-semigroup} and~\ref{thm:cyclic-sparsity},
proved below.  Assuming them, the first calculation determines the constant: by
\eqref{eq:resource-count} and \eqref{eq:candidate-reference-degree},
\[
 NQ_{D_\star}(1)
 \sim\frac{n^kp_\star}{k!}
 \left(\frac{r(r-1)k!}{\operatorname{aut}(F)}
       n^{m-k}p_\star^{r-1}\right)^{-1/(r-1)}
 =C_F n^{k-1/\rho_F}.
\]
In particular, the handoff density cancels.
Fix the constants $A_r,B_r,R_r$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-host},
and choose $\eta>0$ sufficiently small for the following estimates.
Using the handoff counts recorded in Section~\ref{sec:handoff-inputs},
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic-sparsity} gives
$\chi_{R_r}(\Gamma_\star)\le n^{-1/b+C_{F,R_r}\eta}$,
while Corollary~\ref{cor:near-regular-handoff} gives
$D_\star=n^{b\eta+o(1)}$ and
$M=n^{k-1/\rho_F+r\eta+o(1)}$.
Since $k-1/\rho_F=(kr-m)/(r-1)>0$ (as $F$ is not a matching),
we may take $\eta$ small enough that
$-1/b+(C_{F,R_r}+bA_r)\eta<-2\eta$ and
$-(k-1/\rho_F)+(bB_r-r)\eta<-2\eta$.
Consequently
\[
 D_\star^{A_r}\chi_{R_r}(\Gamma_\star)
 +\frac{D_\star^{B_r}}M
 =o(D_\star^{-2/b}).
\]

On $\mathcal G_\star$ the corollary also gives
$\delta_n:=\max_e|d_e/D_\star-1|\le n^{-c_0}$
for some $c_0=c_0(F,\eta)>0$, and
$N=n^{k-1/\rho_F+\eta+o(1)}\le D_\star^K$ for a fixed $K$.
Put $s=\max\{|f\cap g|:f,g\in E(F),\ f\ne g\}$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:resource-semigroup} gives, for every fixed $q>2$,
\[
 \|e^{-(r-1)t\mathsf T}\|_{L^q(\pi)\to L^q(\pi)}
 \le C_{F,\eta,q}(1+t)^{s+1}
 \qquad(0\le t\le T_{D_\star}).
\]
Choose $q$ sufficiently large that
$(k-1/\rho_F+\eta+1)/q<\tfrac12\min\{c_0,b\eta\}$.
Then
\[
 N^{1/q}\left(\delta_n+\frac{\log D_\star}{D_\star}\right)
 (1+\log D_\star)^{2s+4}=o(1).
\]
These are the three hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-host}.

Put $N_\star=\binom nk-ri^\star$, so $N=N_\star$ on
$\mathcal G_\star$.  The matching theorem and the conditional
random-priority representation above give a deterministic
$\epsilon_n\to0$ such that
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left.
  \left(\frac{e(H_{\mathrm{fin}})}{N_\star Q_{D_\star}(1)}-1\right)^2
  \right|\mathcal F_{i^\star}\right]\le\epsilon_n
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal G_\star.
\]
Since $N_\star Q_{D_\star}(1)/n^{k-1/\rho_F}\to C_F$ and 
$\mathbb P(\mathcal G_\star^c) \le\exp\{-(\log n)^{4/3}\}$
we conclude that
\[
 \mathbb E\left[\left(
 \frac{e(H_{\mathrm{fin}})}{n^{k-1/\rho_F}}-C_F
 \right)^2\right] =o(1).
 \qedhere
\]

$|f\cap g|=j$, precisely $j!(k-j)!=k!/\binom kj$

\[

 \sum_{\substack{(f,g)\in E(F)^2\\f\ne g,\ |f\cap g|=j}}
 \sum_{\substack{\sigma:f\overset\sim\longrightarrow e\\
                 \sigma(f\cap g)=J}}\Phi_{F,\sigma}.
\]

summands have the same estimate.  There are $r(r-1)\lambda_j$
role pairs.  Dividing by the resource degree estimate
\eqref{eq:resource-degrees} proves the lemma.

label: eq:exact-intersection-decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\mathsf T_j$ for the part of $\mathsf T$ moving between
resources with intersection size $j$.  Exactly,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-intersection-decomposition}
 (\mathsf T_jh)(e)=\sum_{J\in\binom ej}
   \frac{s_J(e)}{(r-1)d_e}(K_Jh)(e).
\end{equation}
Put $\mathsf K_jh(e)=\binom kj^{-1}\sum_{J\in\binom ej}K_Jh(e)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:role-counts}, Jensen's inequality and the
comparison $\sigma_J=(1+O(n^{-c}))\tau_J$ give
$\|\mathsf T_j-\lambda_j\mathsf K_j\|_{2\to2}\le n^{-c}$.
Indeed, after sampling $e\sim\pi_k$ and then a uniform
$J\subset e$ of size $j$, the conditional law of $e$ is $\tau_J$;
this converts the averaged fibre $L^2$ norms into the global norm.

In the same sampling, $\mathsf U_j^{(k)}\mathsf D_j^{(k)}h(e)$
is the average over $J\in\binom ej$ of $\mathbb E_{\tau_J}h$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre-mixing}, the equivalence of $\sigma_J$
and $\tau_J$, and Jensen therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\|\mathsf K_jh-\mathsf U_j^{(k)}\mathsf D_j^{(k)}h\|_{L^2(\pi_k)}^2\\
 &\quad\le\sum_J\pi_j(J)
   \|K_Jh-\mathbb E_{\tau_J}h\|_{L^2(\tau_J)}^2
 \le n^{-2c}\sum_J\pi_j(J)\|h\|_{L^2(\tau_J)}^2
 =n^{-2c}\|h\|_{L^2(\pi_k)}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Summing over the finitely many occurring values of $j$ proves
\eqref{eq:resource-walk-approx}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
$\beta_\ell=\binom s\ell\binom{k-s}{s-\ell}/\binom ks$.
A step of $\mathsf D\mathsf U$ chooses $\ell$ with probability
$\beta_\ell$, then a uniformly chosen $\ell$-subset $J$ of $S$,
then follows $\mathsf L_J^{(\ell)}$.  When $\ell=s$ the step is
the identity, with mass $1/\binom ks$ in both walks.
For $\ell<s$, replace $\mathsf L_J^{(\ell)}$ by
$\Pi_J^{(s)}$.  Sampling $S\sim\pi_s$ and then $J$
gives conditional law $S\sim\nu_J$.  Jensen's inequality
and Lemma~\ref{lem:shadow-fibre} bound the change in $L^2$
by $n^{-c}$.

For the complete $k$-graph, the analogous exact-$J$ kernel is
uniform on $T$ with $S\cap T=J$, since the number of
containing $k$-edges depends only on $|S\cup T|=2s-\ell$.
This law differs in row total variation by $O_k(n^{-1})$
from uniform on all $s$-sets containing $J$.  Both kernels are
reversible for that uniform law, so duality and interpolation
also give an $O_k(n^{-1})$ bound in $L^2$.
By \eqref{eq:uniform-shadow-law}, $\nu_J$ is pointwise
$1+O(n^{-c})$ times this uniform law.  Applying the same
conditional Jensen bound compares the replaced transitions
with $\overline{\mathsf D\mathsf U}$ in $L^2(\pi_s)$ by $n^{-c}$.
The triangle inequality proves \eqref{eq:shadow-compare-goal}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Call a matrix on $\Omega_s$ \emph{intersection-invariant} if its
$(S,T)$ entry depends only on $|S\cap T|$.  Such matrices form a
vector space of dimension at most $s+1$.  Their products are
intersection-invariant, since permuting $[n]$ merely relabels
the summation variable.  They are also symmetric; hence their
products are symmetric, so any two such matrices commute.

Both $\overline{\mathsf R}_s$ and
$\overline{\mathsf D\mathsf U}$ are intersection-invariant,
Markov and positive semidefinite on the uniform slice: each is
a conditional averaging map followed by its adjoint, or a
convex combination of such maps.  Thus they commute, and
$H:=\overline{\mathsf R}_s\,\overline{\mathsf D\mathsf U}$
is symmetric, positive semidefinite and Markov.  Its eigenvalues
therefore lie in $[0,1]$.

Every power of $H$ is intersection-invariant, so $H$ has at most
$s+1$ distinct eigenvalues $\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_{d-1}$.
Newton interpolation of $f(x)=e^{-ux}$ at these nodes gives
\[
 e^{-uH}
 =\sum_{h=0}^{d-1}f[\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_h]
   \prod_{i=0}^{h-1}(H-\theta_i I).
\]
The divided-difference mean-value theorem gives
$|f[\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_h]|\le u^h/h!$ on $[0,1]$.
Since $H$ is Markov, $\|H-\theta_i I\|_{q\to q}\le2$.
Taking norms yields
\[
 \|e^{-uH}\|_{q\to q}
 \le\sum_{h=0}^{d-1}\frac{(2u)^h}{h!}
 \le\sum_{h=0}^s\frac{(2u)^h}{h!}
 \le(1+2u)^s,
\]
which is (C).

body_md:
\label{lem:persistent-chain-count}
For each $j$ with $\lambda_j>0$, sufficiently long $F$-chains
retaining $J$ are strictly balanced with root $I=e_0\cup e_L$,
uniformly over their ordered role sequences.  For sufficiently
small fixed $\eta$ there is a fixed length
$L_j=O_F(\eta^{-1})$ such that all these chains have at most

name: Endpoint-rooted chain counts

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $I\subsetneq U\subsetneq V(C_L)$.
If $U$ meets some intermediate edge only in $J$, the reversed suffix
supplies the full excess $c_j$.  Otherwise every incomplete block
pays a positive deficit proportional to its missing vertices, which
beats that fixed excess when the chain is sufficiently long.

With $s_i=|U\cap W_i|$, let $q_i$ count the edges of
$C_L[U]$ in $E(F_i)\setminus\{e_{i-1}\}$ and put
\[
 \delta_i=\rho s_i-q_i\ge0,\qquad
 \Delta=\sum_i\delta_i,\qquad
 x=|U|-|I|,\qquad y=X_L-x=La-\sum_i s_i.
\]
As $e(C_L[I])=2$, we have
\[
 e(C_L[U])-2=\sum_iq_i-1=\rho x+c_j-\Delta.
\]
By \eqref{eq:chain-parameters}, strict rooted balance for this
$U$ is therefore equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reuse-surplus}
 \Delta X_L>c_jy.
\end{equation}

If $U\cap e_h=J$ for some $1\le h<L$, apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:one-ended-balance} to the \emph{reversed suffix}
rooted at $e_L$.  Its vertices retained outside $e_L$ number
$j+\sum_{i>h}s_i-k$, and its tested edges retained outside $e_L$
number $\sum_{i>h}q_i-1$.  Thus
$\sum_{i>h}\delta_i\ge\rho(k-j)-1=c_j$.
Since $x>0$ implies $y<X_L$, this proves
\eqref{eq:reuse-surplus}.

Otherwise $U\cap e_h\supsetneq J$ for every $1\le h<L$.
Whenever $s_i<a$ we have $s_i>0$: for $i<L$ this follows from
the presence of a vertex of $e_i\setminus J$, and for $i=L$
from $e_L\subset I$.  If $q_i=0$, then $\delta_i=\rho s_i>0$.
If $q_i>0$, adjoining the incoming edge and applying the strict
part of \eqref{eq:original-template-balance} gives $\delta_i>0$.
There are only finitely many local role pairs and vertex subsets,
so some $\gamma_{F,j}>0$ satisfies
$\delta_i\ge\gamma_{F,j}(a-s_i)$ whenever $s_i<a$.
Hence $\Delta\ge\gamma_{F,j}y$, which gives
\eqref{eq:reuse-surplus} as soon as $X_L>c_j/\gamma_{F,j}$.
This threshold is uniform over role sequences.  If $U=I$
there are no free vertices, and if $U=V(C_L)$ we have equality,
as required.

Finally, at $p_\star=n^{-1/\rho+\eta}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponent-chain-weight}
 \log_n\widehat\phi_{C_L,I}(i^\star)
 =-c_j/\rho+\eta(Lb-1)+o(1).
\end{equation}
Choose a fixed $L_j$ above the balance threshold so that this
exponent exceeds $1$ by a positive constant.  Then
$L_j=O_F(\eta^{-1})$ and $|V(C_{L_j})|\le\eta^{-4}$
for small $\eta$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:JK-cutoff-adapter} and the
balanced-template count \eqref{eq:JK-balanced-count} apply
uniformly to these finitely many decorated templates and all their
root injections.

label: eq:resource-fibre-uniform
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $j,J$ and the fixed length $L=L_j$ from
Lemma~\ref{lem:persistent-chain-count}; put $m_J=|\mathcal R_J|$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:role-counts} and \eqref{eq:resource-degrees} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:resource-fibre-uniform}
 \sigma_J(e)=\frac{1+O(n^{-c})}{m_J}
 \qquad(e\in\mathcal R_J).
\end{equation}
The one-edge rooted count at $J$ gives
$m_J=(1+O(n^{-c}))\binom{n-j}{k-j}p_\star$;
its trajectory is polynomially large since $c_j>0$.
For $e\supset J$ and $x\in e\setminus J$, the enlarged-root
bound \eqref{eq:JK-enlarged-root-count} gives
\[
 |\{f\in\mathcal R_J:x\in f\}|
 \le(1+\log n)^{O_F(1)}\max\{1,n^{k-j-1}p_\star\}.
\]
Indeed the least trajectory after also prescribing $x$ is
$\min\{n,n^{k-j}p_\star\}$.  Dividing by $m_J$ shows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nongeneric-intersection}
 \frac{|\{f\in\mathcal R_J:e\cap f\supsetneq J\}|}{m_J}
 \le (1+\log n)^{O_F(1)}
 \bigl(n^{-1}+(n^{k-j}p_\star)^{-1}\bigr)\le n^{-c}.
\end{equation}
Thus $G_e=\{f\in\mathcal R_J:e\cap f=J\}$ has
$|G_e|=(1+O(n^{-c}))m_J$.

Expand $K_J^L(e,f)$ over its successive copies of $F$.
A nongeneric trajectory has a first step at which a new copy
uses a previously exposed vertex outside its incoming role edge.
Prescribing that vertex costs a factor $n^{-c}$ in the
single-copy rooted extension count: for a proper rooted subtemplate
with tested edges this follows from strict $k$-balance, for one
with no new edge from its additional vertex, and for the full
copy from the factor $n^{b\eta}$.  The enlarged-root estimate
\eqref{eq:JK-enlarged-root-count}, normalised by the
unrestricted count $n^ap_\star^b$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:role-counts}, therefore makes the conditional
probability of each first reuse at most $n^{-c}$.
As $L$ and the number of previously exposed vertices are bounded,
the total nongeneric row mass is $O(n^{-c})$.

For $f\in G_e$, label the $L$ copies of a generic chain,
choose their ordered incoming and outgoing role edges, and
identify consecutive role edges along the common $J$.
These choices give finitely many decorated templates, each with
$X_L$ free vertices and $Q_L$ tested edges.  The number of
compatible root bijections depends only on $k,j$, not on
$(e,f)$, and every generic ordered trajectory has the same
multiplicity $\operatorname{aut}(F)^L$ among these labelled
embeddings.  Lemma~\ref{lem:persistent-chain-count} estimates
each rooted count by $(1+O(n^{-c}))n^{X_L}p_\star^{Q_L}$.
It follows that the number of generic trajectories from $e$ to
$f$ is $(1+O(n^{-c}))a_{n,j,L}$, for a positive constant
$a_{n,j,L}$ independent of the endpoints.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:role-counts} and \eqref{eq:resource-degrees},
each step denominator is
$(1+O(n^{-c}))(r-1)\lambda_jD_\star/\binom kj$.
Hence the generic contribution to $K_J^L(e,f)$ is
$(1+O(n^{-c}))b_{n,j,L}$ on $G_e$ and zero elsewhere,
with $b_{n,j,L}>0$ independent of $e,f$.

Put $\varepsilon=n^{-c}$, decreasing $c$ if necessary.
Every row of $K_J^L$ has exceptional mass $O(\varepsilon)$;
its generic mass is $(1+O(\varepsilon))b_{n,j,L}$ at each
of $(1+O(\varepsilon))m_J$ good endpoints.
As the rows sum to one,
$b_{n,j,L}=(1+O(\varepsilon))/m_J$.  Together with
\eqref{eq:resource-fibre-uniform}, this gives
\[
 \sup_e\sum_f|K_J^L(e,f)-\sigma_J(f)|=O(\varepsilon).
\]
We deduce $\|K_J^L-\Pi_J\|_{\infty\to\infty}=O(\varepsilon)$
and so $\|K_J^L-\Pi_J\|_{2\to2}=O(\varepsilon)$ by self-adjointness.

title: Proof

Suppose a proper rooted subtemplate retains $q>0$ of the
resource edges, forming $c$ intervals of positions.  Let $h$
be the number of these intervals that touch an endpoint of the
chain.  Here $h\le2$ and $c-h\ge0$, since an interval touching

force all $qf$ of their private vertices and at least

outside the prescribed root.  They therefore force at least
\[

 =q(k-s)+(c-h)(s-\ell)\ge q(k-s)
\]
non-root vertices.  This bounds their density by $1/(k-s)$.
A subtemplate with no tested edges has density zero.
The full chain has $L$ tested edges and
\eqref{eq:shadow-chain-free} free vertices, giving
\eqref{eq:shadow-chain-strict-balance}.

labelled embeddings of \eqref{eq:shadow-chain-definition},
independent of its endpoints: the labels order the intermediate
$U_i$ and the private $P_i$.  The rooted chain count above gives
the common trajectory $n^{X_L}p_\star^L$, with relative error
$n^{-c}$.  Hence the number of generic ordered trajectories
from any $S_0$ to any $S_L\in G_{S_0}$ is
$(1+O(n^{-c}))a_{n,\ell,L}$ for one positive number
$a_{n,\ell,L}$ independent of the endpoints.

In the expansion of \eqref{eq:lower-shadow-kernel}, each step
has weight
\[
 \frac{d_e}{\binom{k-s}{s-\ell}\sum_{g\supset S}d_g}
 =\frac{1+O(n^{-c})}
 {\binom{k-s}{s-\ell}\binom{n-s}{k-s}p_\star},
\]
by \eqref{eq:resource-degrees} and
the one-edge handoff count.  The generic contribution to
the $L$-step endpoint transition is therefore
$(1+O(n^{-c}))b_{n,\ell,L}$ on $G_{S_0}$, independent of
$S_0,S_L$, and zero outside $G_{S_0}$.

The same row-sum argument as in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:fibre-mixing} now makes the common generic
transition weight $(1+O(n^{-c}))/m_J$.
The exceptional mass is $O(n^{-c})$, so the rows of
$(\mathsf L_J^{(\ell)})^L$ differ from $\nu_J$ in total variation
by $O(n^{-c})$. This gives an $L^\infty$ bound, so by self-adjointness we deduce
\[
 \|\mathsf L_J^{(\ell)}-\Pi_J^{(s)}\|_{L^2(\nu_J)\to L^2(\nu_J)}
 \le n^{-c/L}.
\]
This proves Lemma~\ref{lem:shadow-fibre}, and hence completes
the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:resource-semigroup}.

name: Short-cycle candidate bound

label: lem:cyclic-type-count
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cyclic-type-count}
Let $S$ be a fixed self-avoiding cyclic $F$-union with
$|V(S)|\le\eta^{-4}$.  On $\mathcal G_\star$, the number of embeddings
of $S$ into $H_\star$ is at most
\[
 \#\{S\hookrightarrow H_\star\}
 \le n^{k-1/\rho-1/b+O_{F,S}(\eta)}.
\]
head: environment
name: Bounded cyclic-type count

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $R\ge4$.  A simple incidence cycle of length $2\ell\le R$
in $\Gamma_\star$ alternates between distinct candidates and distinct
resources.  Its candidates are therefore distinct copies
$F_1,\ldots,F_\ell$ of $F$, while its resources are distinct
$k$-edges $e_1,\ldots,e_\ell$ with
$e_i\in E(F_i)\cap E(F_{i+1})$ (cyclic indices).  Hence the
union $S=\bigcup_{i=1}^\ell F_i$ is exactly a self-avoiding cyclic
$F$-union in the sense defined above, including when $\ell=2$ or when
there are further overlaps.  It has at most $mR/2$ ordinary vertices.
There are finitely many isomorphism types of such unions, depending
only on $F,R$, and for each embedded union only $O_{F,R}(1)$ choices of
the ordered candidates, shared resources, incidence cycle and a candidate
on that cycle.  Consequently the number of candidates on short cycles satisfies
the explicit finite-type bound
\[
 M\chi_R(\Gamma_\star)
 \le O_{F,R}(1)
 \sum_{\substack{S\text{ a cyclic }F\text{-union type}\\
                    v(S)\le mR/2}}
 \#\{S\hookrightarrow H_\star\}.
\]
Take $\eta$ sufficiently small for the finite collection of union types.  Summing the bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:cyclic-type-count} over the
finitely many types bounds the number of candidates on cycles of
length at most $R$ by
\(
 n^{k-1/\rho-1/b+O_{F,R}(\eta)}.
\)
Corollary~\ref{cor:near-regular-handoff} gives
$M=n^{k-1/\rho+r\eta+o(1)}$; dividing by $M$ gives \eqref{eq:short-cycle-target}.

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Uniform handoff event for bounded templates

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply \cite[Sections~5--7, Lemmas~7.14 and~7.16, and Lemma~10.1]{JoosKuhn}
to the complete initial $k$-graph.  Every bounded rooted template has
initial count $(1+O(n^{-1}))\widehat\phi_{A,I}(0)$, so the common
stopping event controls all the required templates and root injections.
The choice $\varepsilon_{\rm JK}=2\eta^2<\eta$ places $i^\star$ before
the controlled horizon; their Lemma~10.1 gives the exceptional
probability.  Their balanced counts, strictly balanced upper bounds,
and enlarged-root bounds give (ii)--(iv), and the rooted copy-degree
estimate gives (i).  In (iv), prescribing additional vertices of $J$
does not change the tested-edge set $E(A)\setminus E(A[I])$.

label: lem:JK-cutoff-adapter
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:JK-cutoff-adapter}
For fixed $F,\eta$ there is a choice of $\delta_{\rm JK}>0$,
depending only on $F,\eta$ and compatible with
Proposition~\ref{prop:JK-handoff}, such that the following holds
\emph{simultaneously}.  Let $(A,I)$ be any balanced rooted template
with at least one edge outside $A[I]$ and $|V(A)|\le\eta^{-4}$.
If, for some fixed $\xi>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:JK-positive-trajectory}
 \widehat\phi_{A,I}(i^\star)\ge n^\xi,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:JK-cutoff-check}
 i^\star<i_{A,I}^{\delta_{\rm JK}^{1/2}}.
\end{equation}
Consequently Proposition~\ref{prop:JK-handoff}(ii) gives a
polynomially small relative error for $\Phi_{A,\psi}$, uniformly
over all applicable templates and prescribed root injections.

name: Polynomial trajectory lies before the balanced cutoff

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $q=e(A)-e(A[I])\ge1$ and $t=|V(A)|-|I|$.
The terminal trajectory has exponent
\[
 \widehat\phi_{A,I}(i^\star)
 =n^{t-q/\rho+q\eta+o(1)}.
\]
Since the template order is at most $\eta^{-4}$, all positive
exponents $t-q/\rho+q\eta$ have a common positive lower bound.  Write $\delta=\delta_{\rm JK}$.
Since
\[
 \zeta(i^\star)^{-\delta^{1/2}}
 =n^{(\rho\eta/2-\eta^2)\delta^{1/2}+o(1)},
\]
we may choose $\delta$ once, sufficiently small in terms of $F,\eta$,
so that the exponent on the right is below half this common lower
bound and $q>\rho\delta^{1/2}/2$ holds for every $q\ge1$.
Up to a factor independent of $i$, the ratio
$\widehat\phi_{A,I}(i)/\zeta(i)^{-\delta^{1/2}}$
is then a positive power of $\widehat p(i)$; it decreases as the
process advances.  At $i^\star$ the ratio is bigger than one, and
therefore \eqref{eq:JK-cutoff-check} holds simultaneously for all the templates in the
statement.  Decreasing $\delta$ further if necessary also meets the
conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:JK-handoff}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S$ be a cyclic $F$-union. Lemma~12.5 in \cite{JoosKuhn} gives a
resource edge $e$ with $\rho_{S,e}>\rho=b/a$.  The integer surplus is
therefore
\[
 a(e(S)-1)-b(v(S)-k)\ge1,
 \qquad
 v(S)-e(S)/\rho\le k-1/\rho-1/b.
\]
The exponent $k-1/\rho-1/b$ is positive: strict balance excludes a
matching, so some two role edges meet and $\rho\ge1/(k-1)$, giving
$k-1/\rho-1/b\ge1-1/b>0$.

By \cite[Lemmas~12.2 and~12.3]{JoosKuhn}, either $(S,\varnothing)$
is strictly balanced or it contains a proper unrooted subtemplate $B$
that is strictly balanced with $e(B)/v(B)\ge\rho$, chosen with
maximum density and minimum vertex count.  In the second case every
extension root $J\supseteq V(B)$ has density $\rho_{S,J}\ge\rho$.

In the first case the strictly balanced handoff bound from
Proposition~\ref{prop:JK-handoff}(iii) gives
\[
 \#\{S\hookrightarrow H_\star\}
 \le(1+\log n)^{O_{F,S}(1)}n^{v(S)}p_\star^{e(S)}
 \le(1+\log n)^{O_{F,S}(1)}
     n^{k-1/\rho-1/b+O_{F,S}(\eta)}.
\]
In the second case the same handoff bound counts $B$ in at most
$(1+\log n)^{O_{F,S}(1)}n^{O_{F,S}(\eta)}$ ways.  
By \cite[Lemma~12.6]{JoosKuhn}, using the upper bound
in Proposition~\ref{prop:JK-handoff}(iii), gives at most another
$(1+\log n)^{O_{F,S}(1)}n^{O_{F,S}(\eta)}$ completions:
the density condition $\rho_{S,J}\ge\rho$ is retained when the root
is enlarged during that induction.
